title: Why is the Mona Lisa so famous?
subject: art
description: It is the most famous painting in the world. Yet in 1503, its own painter had better things to do than the portrait of a merchant's wife.
author: dusan-nikolic

hero.hook: The most looked-at painting on the planet may have been, for Leonardo, a side job.

blocks.text: For one of the most famous paintings in the world, very little is known for certain about the *Mona Lisa*. Art historians agree on the essentials: Leonardo da Vinci painted it in Florence between **1503 and 1506**. In **1517**, he carried it with him to France, and the panel ended up in the collection of King [[Francis I]].

Legends have filled the historical vacuum. The painting is spoken of as a woman, "she." Her half-smile is called mysterious. After the theft of **1911**, even its authenticity was questioned. All these stories made its fame, but they pushed its context aside. Yet at the time Leonardo painted it, the work may not have mattered to him at all.

Art historians widely accept that the sitter is [[Lisa Gherardini]], wife of **Francesco del Giocondo**, a merchant and minor figure in the Florentine government. Hence the painting's other name, *La Gioconda*. The identification rests on the biography of Leonardo published by [[Giorgio Vasari]] in **1550** and again in **1568**, in his *Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects*.

blocks.caption: Vasari's Lives, Florentine edition of 1568: the text that gives the sitter a name.

blocks.text: Why did Francesco commission the portrait? Nobody knows. Leonardo started work in early **1503**. What happened next is still debated: for historians, Vasari's account reads like a literary invention, a biographer filling the blanks with a good story. In mid-**1506**, Leonardo left Florence for Milan in search of better employment. The unfinished portrait went with him.

According to Vasari, Leonardo hired musicians and jesters to keep his sitter entertained during the sittings. Historians see this as the biographer's invention, but it is the story that launched the myth of the "Mona Lisa smile."

In October **1503**, the Florentine government hired Leonardo to paint the [[Battle of Anghiari]] in the [[Palazzo Vecchio]], the seat of the Florentine Republic. The mural was to commemorate Florence's victory over Milan in **1440**. In the Renaissance, a history scene counted for far more than a portrait. Alongside religious, mythological and allegorical subjects, it was seen as the highest form of art.

blocks.caption: Rubens's copy of the central melee: the only trace of the great unfinished mural in the Palazzo Vecchio.

blocks.text: Next to a large public commission, the private portrait of a minor official's wife carried little weight. From December **1503**, Leonardo spent more and more time preparing the large composition. Prestige and better pay: the Mona Lisa could wait. By the end of his second stay in Florence, the portrait was unfinished. So was the *Battle of Anghiari*: only preparatory sketches and their copies survive.
It is possible that only the landscape in the background was still unfinished when Leonardo left for Milan in 1506.

Leonardo died on **May 2, 1519**, in Amboise, France. The *Mona Lisa* never reached the Giocondo family. After the French Revolution, the royal collection became public and the painting entered the **Louvre**. Since the early 19th century, its smile has been described in a thousand ways, from divine to sensual.

blocks.caption: The front page of Excelsior in January 1914: the Mona Lisa returns after the theft of 1911.

blocks.text: The turning point was the theft of the painting from the museum in **1911**. Newspapers turned the Mona Lisa into a worldwide sensation. Ever since, popular journalism and fiction have routinely questioned the work's authenticity and the sitter's identity, without any grounding in proper historical analysis. The painting has become the center of ever more stories, ones we still hear today.

sections.title: A painting that outgrew its author

blocks.text: More than **500 years** after the portrait was begun, Lisa del Giocondo is more attractive than ever. Placed behind bulletproof glass at the Louvre, the painting is cut off from its historical context. Freed from it, it has acquired the status of a universal icon. That status has a price: in modern times, no restoration has been attempted.

events.title: The theft
events.detail: The press turns the Mona Lisa into a worldwide sensation.

blocks.text: Removing the [[varnish]] yellowed by the centuries, the protective coat used in oil painting, would risk damaging the work. And even if a restoration went well, there is a fear that the *Mona Lisa* would lose its hold on us. Leonardo's original technique and coloring matter less than the image. Now a vessel for countless stories, the painting has outgrown its author and art history.
Set aside in 1503 for a more prestigious commission, the *Mona Lisa* owes its status as an icon to five centuries of legends and a theft, far more than to the rank Leonardo gave it.
